title: Spin a tin humming top: stand it up, pump its plunger, and let go so it spins alone for ten seconds
instruction: Stand the top up by its knob, pump the knob down and up until the top spins fast, then let go and keep both grippers clear so it spins on its point by itself for ten seconds.
context: A tin humming top is a toy most people have spun: push the knob on its twisted rod down and the tin body turns, lift the knob and it freewheels, so a few quick pumps build the spin, and then the hand has to leave without knocking it. Here the top lies stopped on its side. With one hand, as a person does it, the robot takes the knob, stands the top on its point, and pumps the knob down and up while that same grip keeps the top upright; then it opens the gripper and lifts straight off. The top is top-heavy and stands only while it spins fast. Each stroke has to go straight down the rod (a sideways pull skates the point across the tray), the strokes have to get faster as the body speeds up (a slow push no longer catches the screw), and the release must not nudge it. The number of strokes is free: only the time the top then spins alone is scored.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table. 1) Tray: IKEA TILLGANG (104.199.50), 370 x 290, gray, centred at (195, 50), long side along x; deck 3 thick, rim 12 high (estimates). 2) Top: Schylling Little Tin Tops (MTA) tin humming top, 127 across, listed height 139.7, about 110 g (estimate); red knob 28 across on a twisted rod with 80 travel (estimates). Its red plastic point is a round button of radius 4.8, an estimate from the product photo: before trials lay calipers across the point's round end (9 to 10) or hold a 4.5 to 5 radius gauge against it; a sharper point is a different toy for this task. The top starts stopped, knob pushed in, lying on its point and rim (leaning about 44 degrees toward +y) with the point at (120, 50). One white ink dot on the tin shows its turning. No collar, stand or fixture. Both arms start at ready with open grippers; the scripted demonstration uses the left arm only and the right arm stays at ready.
scoring: Judged from the trial video (60 frames per second or more) with a stopwatch. Free-spin time t is the longest unbroken stretch in which both grippers are at least 5 cm from every part of the top while the top turns on its point by itself: at least one turn per second (white dot), its tin rim off the tray, its point on the tray's flat deck at least 10 mm in from the tray's rim. 0: the top was never brought to one turn per second by pushing its knob down (doing nothing scores 0; twisting the tin itself does not count), or it left the table, or the rod was pulled out of its guide or bent. 0.25: spun by the plunger, t under 2 s (fell at once, touched, or never let go). 0.5: 2 s <= t < 5 s. 0.75: 5 s <= t < 10 s. 1.0: t >= 10 s. So exactly 2, 5 and 10 s score 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0. The number of strokes is not scored. The run ends when t reaches 10 s.
reset_notes: About 30 seconds. Wait for the top to stop or stop it by hand, push the knob in, and lay the top back on its point and rim with the point on its mark at (120, 50), leaning toward +y. Check the knob and rod are straight, the tray is dry and on its marks, both arms at ready with open grippers. First preparation, about two minutes (estimate): remove the tag and string, wipe the tray, put one white ink dot on the tin for counting turns on video, check the point with calipers or a radius gauge (9 to 10 mm across its round end), and stand the top on a kitchen scale and push the knob down steadily: the reading should rise by roughly 1.4 kg (the 14 N screw push is an estimate). No per-trial consumables. Top $11.99 and tray $1.99 at published prices, marker about $2 (estimate).
fidelity: Rigid tin shell on a round point; nothing holds it upright and no spin is added. A per-substep rule stands for the one-way screw: pushing the rod meets about 14 N and gives the shell at most 0.7 of the hand's work; lifting freewheels. The point's 4.8 mm radius is an estimate from the product photo and free-spin time depends strongly on it (a 2.5 mm point fell within 7 s). The simulated top leans over below about 11 turns per second, sooner than a real one. The rest are estimates. No sound.
